plan.paradox: A penny gets you a whole record club.
plan.odd_fact: If you stay silent, the next album ships with a full-price bill. Sounds generous.
plan.twist: But it forces a paid shipment, the negative-option trick.
plan.cause: The penny sign-up locks a minimum purchase; missing the opt-out deadline automatically adds a full-price album, fueling $1.4 billion revenue in 1996.
plan.everyday: Bakery offers: free cupcake with any pastry, but you must buy two pastries at regular price; miss the checkout deadline and a $5 cake is added. Gym: $1 day-pass, then you must attend three classes at full price; skip the sign-out and a $30 membership bill arrives. Streaming app: $0.99 trial month, then you're enrolled in a $12 monthly plan unless you cancel before month's end. In each case the "free" lure pushes the costly commitment, making the paid option feel like the smart choice.
plan.rule: Watch for a tiny upfront cost that hides an automatic charge. Follow for more.

beats.say: A penny gets you a whole record club.
Sign up and you receive 12 records for a penny.
Or you can join the regular plan with no upfront discount.
A third tier promises a free bonus album after the first shipment.
If you don't say no by the deadline, the next album ships with a full-price bill. Sounds generous.
But it forces a paid shipment, the negative-option trick.
The penny sign-up obligates a minimum purchase; missing the opt-out automatically adds a full-price album.
That automatic album generated $1.4 billion in 1996, then collapsed to $17 million by 2014.
When the deadline passes, the club silently turns a free promise into a bill.
You see it everywhere: a bakery gives a free cupcake but adds a $5 cake if you don't cancel.
A gym sells a $1 day pass, then enrolls you in a $30 membership unless you opt out.
A streaming app offers a $0.99 trial, then locks you into $12 a month unless you cancel.
Watch for a tiny upfront cost that hides an automatic charge. Follow for more.
